paras: The threatened lynching of Charlie Word took place in San Antonio, Texas, in August 1881, when a one-legged Black man accused of assaulting a German girl was jailed before, according to the reports, a crowd could lynch him. No attack on him is reported, and the story ran in Texas papers and, without his name, in papers in Washington and Pennsylvania.

According to a special to the Dallas Herald dated San Antonio, August 22, early on the previous morning Charlie Word, described as a 'one-legged negro', was accused of committing 'an outrage upon the person' of a German girl named Dora Ellerman in the suburbs of the city. The dispatch said she was beaten about the head and body and lay insensible for a long time. A separate special to the Galveston News, also from San Antonio, did not name the man but said he knocked the girl down with his crutch as she walked home from mass.

Word was arrested and jailed, and the Herald's correspondent wrote that he was taken to jail 'quietly or he would have been lynched by an incensed crowd'. The Galveston News version put the arrest on August 22 and said he was lodged in jail 'before his crime was generally known, else it is thought he would have been summarily dealt with'. Neither account reports a crowd gathering at the jail.
No report of an indictment, trial or other outcome appears in the coverage, which ends with the reprints of August 24 and 25.

The Dallas Daily Herald printed its special on August 23, calling the accused 'the villain' and the assault a 'shameful deed' that had 'created quite a sensation'. The Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman reprinted the same text on August 25 under 'Texas by Telegraph', spelling the names 'Charlie Ward' and 'Dora Ellermann'.

Outside Texas the Galveston News version circulated without names: the Washington Evening Star ran it on August 23 under the head 'Outrage by a One Legged Negro', and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer included it in a crime roundup the next day. All the reports treated the assault as established and mentioned the averted lynching in a single closing sentence without comment.
The accused's surname is 'Word' in the Dallas Herald and 'Ward' in the Austin reprint of the same dispatch, and the girl's surname is spelled 'Ellerman' and 'Ellermann'.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Charlie Word
bases: A Black man accused of assaulting a girl was jailed, and the reports say a crowd would have lynched him otherwise; no attack on him is reported (A1, A2, A4).
No one was killed: the papers report only that a crowd would have lynched the accused had he not been jailed quietly (A1, A4) or before the crime was known (A2), so at most a threatened lynching.
Two separate San Antonio dispatches, the Herald special (A1, reprinted as A4) and the Galveston News special (A2, reprinted as A3), agree on the accusation, the arrest and the averted lynching.

accounts.label: Dallas Herald special from San Antonio
accounts.gist: Early on Aug. 21 a one-legged Black man, Charlie Word, assaulted Dora Ellerman in the suburbs; he was jailed quietly, or an incensed crowd would have lynched him.

accounts.label: Galveston News special from San Antonio
accounts.gist: An unnamed one-legged Black man was arrested on Aug. 22 for knocking down a young German girl with his crutch on her way home from mass; he was jailed before the crime was generally known, 'else it is thought' he would have been 'summarily dealt with'.

framing.detail: The Herald special calls him 'the villain' and treats the assault as established while reporting the averted lynching without comment.
The Austin weekly reprinted the same text under 'Texas by Telegraph'.
The Washington Evening Star ran the Galveston News version under the head 'Outrage by a One Legged Negro' in a 'Texas Topics' column; the Lancaster Intelligencer reprinted it in a crime roundup.

info: The alleged assault took place early on the morning of Sunday, August 21, 1881 ('early yesterday morning' in an Aug. 22 dispatch); A2 says the arrest was made 'to-day', Aug. 22.
Charlie Word (A1) or Charlie Ward (A4), described as a 'one-legged negro'; A2 does not name him.

Accused of an 'outrage upon the person' of a German girl, Dora Ellerman (Ellermann in A4), beating her about the head and body until she was insensible; A2 says he knocked her down with his crutch as she walked home from mass.
An 'incensed crowd' that, the papers say, would have lynched him; no crowd is reported to have gathered at the jail.
No report of a trial or later outcome was found.
